Avant les empires, il y a les hommes de: Before the empires came the people of the Capsian culture—hunters of the steppes more than eight thousand years ago—followed by the Berbers (Amazighs), an indigenous people organized into Numidian kingdoms. Their hilltop villages and their language still survive today in the south, in Chenini, Douiret, and Tamezret.
Avant même les Français, ce sont les Ita: Even before the French, it was the Italians—Sicilians, Sardinians, and people from Livorno—who formed the largest European community in Tunisia. Fishermen from La Goulette, masons, merchants, doctors, and artists: long outnumbering the French colonists, they have left a lasting mark on the cuisine, architecture, and dialect of Tunis, and have given the capital its Mediterranean and cosmopolitan character.

En 1270, le roi de France Louis IX — Sai: In 1270, King Louis IX of France—Saint Louis—landed on the shores of Carthage at the head of the Eighth Crusade, hoping to win over the Hafsid sultan. But an epidemic ravaged his camp, and the king died there in August 1270. The crusade came to an abrupt end, and a treaty was signed with Tunis. A chapel built later on Byrsa Hill—now known as the Acropolium—serves as a memorial to this event.
En 1574, les Ottomans mettent fin aux Ha: In 1574, the Ottomans brought an end to the Hafsid dynasty and made Tunisia a regency—governed first by deys and pashas, then by beys who gradually gained their autonomy. In 1705, the Husseinid dynasty came to power, ruling until the mid-20th century and building palaces, madrasas, and medinas.
En 1881, la France impose son protectora: In 1881, France established its protectorate. Tunis took on the character of a European city with wide avenues; ports, railroads, and phosphate mines transformed the country. Colonial society was cosmopolitan: Tunisians—
En 670, la conquête arabe fonde Kairouan: In 670, the Arab conquest led to the founding of Kairouan, the first major Muslim city in the Maghreb and a spiritual center. This was followed by the Aghlabids (who built the Great Mosque and the pools), the Fatimids—who set out from Mahdia to conquer Egypt—the Zirids, and then the Hafsids, who made Tunis their capital. Andalusians driven out of Spain repopulated Testour and the north.

Fondée par les Phéniciens venus de Tyr,: Founded by the Phoenicians from Tyre, Carthage became the great maritime power of the western Mediterranean. Its ports, trading posts, and fleet challenged Rome during the Punic Wars—right up to Hannibal and his elephants. In 146 B.C., Rome razed the city to the ground. But other Punic cities, such as Kerkouane, have survived almost intact.

La Tunisie tient dans un mouchoir trois: Tunisia encompasses three worlds within a small area. To the north, the Mediterranean Sea, its capes, and the Kroumirie rainforest. In the center, the Tunisian Mountain Range and its peaks. To the south lies the Sahara: the great erg, the mountain oases of Chebika and Tamerza, and the salt chotts that glisten like mirrors. Between them lies Lake Ichkeul, a global stopover for migratory birds.

: sans doute le seul au monde à porter c: : undoubtedly the only one in the world to bear the name of a local people (whereas America derives its name from a European explorer). And that is just one layer: over three thousand years, between the sea and the desert, nearly all the powers of the Mediterranean have passed through this land—each leaving behind its stones, its words, its tastes, layered one upon another like the strata of a single narrative. Here, in brief, is the history of this land, and the nature that sustains it.
Au XIIe siècle, profitant de l'affaiblis: In the 12th century, taking advantage of the Zirid dynasty’s weakening, the Normans of Sicily, under Roger II, captured Mahdia in 1148 and part of the coastline—Sousse, Sfax, and Gabès. For about a dozen years, a short-lived “Norman Kingdom of Africa” existed, before the Almohads recaptured these cities in 1160. In a curious turn of events, Sicily—which had once been conquered from Ifriqiya—briefly returned the favor.
Dernier acte de la guerre en Afrique du: The final phase of the war in North Africa, the Tunisian Campaign pitted the Allies against Axis forces entrenched in a bridgehead. The fighting was fierce: the Kasserine Pass, where Rommel dealt a severe blow to the Americans in February 1943; the Mareth Line in the south; Medjez el-Bab and Longstop Hill on the road to Tunis; El Guettar and the Akarit Wadi. In May 1943, Tunis and Bizerte fell, and nearly 250,000 Axis soldiers surrendered. Numerous military cemeteries—Commonwealth and German—preserve the memory of these events.
Dès le IIe siècle, l'Afrique romaine dev: As early as the 2nd century, Roman Africa became one of the major centers of Christianity. It was here that Tertullian, the first great Christian author to write in Latin, wrote; it was here, in Carthage in 203, that Saints Perpetua and Felicity were martyred—their story has been passed down to us—and it was here that Bishop Cyprian taught. The region was dotted with basilicas and baptisteries—in Carthage, Sbeïtla, and Haïdra—and was the scene of heated debates, such as the Donatist controversy.
En 439, le roi vandale Genséric s'empare: In 439, the Vandal king Genseric captured Carthage and made it the capital of a Germanic kingdom that dominated the western Mediterranean and sacked Rome itself in 455. A century later, the Byzantine Emperor Justinian sent his general Belisarius to reconquer Africa (533): Carthage became an exarchate of the Eastern Empire. The mighty Byzantine fortresses that still crown Haïdra, Sbeïtla, and Aïn Tounga—the last bastions before the arrival of the Arabs—date from this period.
La Tunisie devient un enjeu du grand due: Tunisia became a key battleground in the great conflict between the Spain of Charles V and the Ottoman Empire. In 1534, the corsair Khayr ad-Din Barbarossa captured Tunis in the name of the sultan; the following year, Charles V recaptured it in a spectacular expedition and established a Spanish garrison at La Goulette, with a Hafsid vassal. For some forty years, Spain held the Gulf of Tunis in its grip—until the Ottoman Empire’s definitive conquest in 1574.
Les Juifs de Tunisie comptent parmi les: The Jews of Tunisia are among the oldest communities in the diaspora: tradition traces the origins of the Ghriba Synagogue in Djerba back to antiquity. Over the centuries, Jews from Spain arrived after 1492, followed by the “Grana” from Livorno during the Ottoman period. Present in the hara of Tunis as well as in the towns of the south—as artisans, merchants, scholars, and goldsmiths—they form a vibrant part of the country. The community dispersed widely in the 20th century, but the annual pilgrimage to the Ghriba keeps its memory alive.
Sur les ruines de Carthage, Rome bâtit l: On the ruins of Carthage, Rome built Proconsular Africa: one of the Empire’s richest provinces, which exported wheat and olive oil to the capital. Theaters, capitolia, thermal baths, and amphitheaters dot the landscape—Dougga, Sbeïtla, Bulla Regia, and the colossal amphitheater at El Jem. It was also a major center of early Christianity, home to the bishop and theologian Cyprian of Carthage.
